title: Rebranding After an Acquisition: A Practical Guide (2026)
description: When to rebrand after an acquisition, what to keep, what to change, what it costs and how to roll it out, with the Airport Executive rebrand under new ownership as the worked example.
body:
Rebranding after an acquisition is the process of deciding what happens to the acquired company’s name, logo and visual identity once ownership changes, and then rolling that decision out across every customer touchpoint.

In my experience the name is usually worth keeping and the logo rarely is, and a new identity should almost never launch in the first 90 days.

This guide is for two readers: you bought a business, or a larger company bought yours.

I rebranded Airport Executive under new ownership: the name stayed after more than 25 years in business, and everything around it changed.

Here are the key takeaways.

  • Verdict: rebrand when the identity no longer fits, refresh a good name that looks dated, keep a brand that is the asset.
  • Five paths: absorb, endorse, keep separate, fuse, or new brand.
  • Timing: decide at close, announce on day one, audit and brief within 60 days, launch in months three to six, finish within a year.
  • Cost: scope (refresh, identity, or identity plus website) sets the budget; implementation is separate.

Should you rebrand after an acquisition?

Rebrand after an acquisition when the acquired identity no longer fits who owns the business or where it is going, refresh when the name has equity but the look is dated, and leave the brand alone when the brand is the asset you bought.

The terms get mixed up, so here is my scale.

  • Refresh: keeps the name and mark, tidies the system (a brand refresh).
  • Redesign: keeps the name, replaces the mark and system.
  • Rename: replaces the name as well as the identity (a full rebrand).
  • Architecture: how the brand sits beside the acquirer, its brand architecture (next section).

Landor’s study of S&P Global 100 deals found 74% of acquired assets rebranded within seven years (78% for deals under $99M, 46% over $5B), so the real questions are how much and when.

You bought the company

Your realistic choice is keep, refresh or redesign under the same name.

At Airport Executive I redesigned under a kept name, and the project is first in my rebranding examples.

A larger company bought yours

Expect absorb or endorse, and ask on day one which it is.

When the brand is the asset, it stays.

Amazon said in its deal announcement that Whole Foods Market would keep its name, headquarters and CEO, and Microsoft promised LinkedIn its brand, culture and independence.

The rebrand should follow a decision about the business, not stand in for one.

What are the brand options after an acquisition?

After an acquisition a brand can be absorbed into the buyer’s brand, endorsed by it, kept separate, fused with it, or replaced by a new brand; keep separate and absorb are the most common outcomes in the data below.

  1. Absorb: the name is retired; T-Mobile retired Sprint on one brand day, August 2, 2020, rebranding thousands of stores in magenta.
  2. Endorse: a parent line is added; Instagram and WhatsApp gained “from Facebook” (2019), then “from Meta”; “Fitbit by Google” (2022) became “Google Fitbit” (2024).
  3. Keep separate: only ownership changes; Amazon kept Whole Foods Market, and Salesforce kept Slack (2021).
  4. Fuse: brand names or marks combine; Kraft Heinz put both wordmarks on one line (2015), and United kept its name but took Continental’s globe (2010).
  5. New brand: both corporate names retire; Stellantis became the umbrella over Fiat, Peugeot and Jeep (2021), while Verizon’s Oath lasted under two years before becoming Verizon Media.
OptionWhat changesWhen it fitsRisk to equity
AbsorbName, logo, site, signageBuyer’s brand is strongerHigh; needs a bridge period
EndorseParent line addedParent adds credibilityMedium; reads as “founders left”
Keep separateBack office onlyThe brand is the assetLow
FuseCombined name or symbolMerger of equalsMedium; committee identity
New brandEverythingNeither name fitsHighest; zero awareness

In post-merger brand architecture terms, absorb is a branded house, endorse is an endorsed brand and keep separate is a house of brands (see the four brand architecture types).

Siegel+Gale’s review of US financial-services deals (2019 to 2023) found 50% kept separate brands, 23% absorbed the acquired company and 4% endorsed it, and a net-new brand appeared in no more than 2% of deals.

A “now part of” line ages badly when the parent name means nothing to the acquired audience, and endorsement is often step one of a multi-year absorption, so decide the end state before the first step.

How long after an acquisition should you rebrand?

Decide the brand path at close, announce it on day one, use the first 30 days to audit what customers recognize, decide and brief by day 60, and launch the new identity on one day between months three and six, with the physical rollout finished within a year.

McKinsey found 65% of the acquirers it surveyed finish the brand transition within 12 months and 80% within 18.

Only about 40% take a fact-based approach to brand positioning, so do the brand strategy and the audit before you design.

On day one, tell employees first, then customers within hours, and say what is not changing (name, team, service, pricing, contacts) before what is.

Bain documents the cost: First Union lost 20% of its customers in the year after buying CoreStates.

Move faster when

Some situations cannot wait.

  • The old name is legally encumbered or did not transfer.
  • The founder’s name is on the door and the founder left.
  • The acquired brand hurts the buyer’s reputation.
  • Customers already confuse the two businesses.

Slow down when

  • Customers search for and refer the old name.
  • Reviews and rankings depend on it.
  • The service team and pricing are still settling.
  • You have not heard what customers call the business.

How do you audit brand equity before a rebrand?

Ask dispatch, reception or sales what customers call the business, read the last 100 reviews for repeated words, check branded queries in Search Console and photograph every touchpoint; within a week you will know whether recognition lives in the name, a color, a symbol or the vehicles.

Separate what has changed operationally from what needs to change visibly.

I check five things (more in my brand audit and brand discovery guides).

  • Recognition: what customers call the business, and the color or symbol they remember.
  • Visual identity: whether the system works from vehicles to invoices.
  • Reputation: what reviews and staff praise or complain about.
  • Confusion: where old-owner references or sister brands overlap.
  • Direction: what the new owners plan that customers will notice.

Pick one anchor element to keep constant, so customers can connect old and new.

The output is one page marking every element keep, refine or replace, signed off before design starts, which later becomes the brief.

What should you keep or change under new ownership?

Keep whatever customers use to find and recognize the business (usually the name, sometimes a color), refresh what is familiar but dated, and replace what is wrong for where the business is going, usually the logo, typography and website.

Judge each element on recognition and fit, not age.

Keep the name when customers search for it

Signal new ownership without renaming through an “under new ownership” message, an endorsement line or a campaign line, because a retained name can still get a completely new identity.

Change the name only for a departing founder’s name, a legal encumbrance or one platform brand, and resolve that with my company name and business name guides before finalizing the identity.

Refine a logo people recognize, replace one they do not

The logo changes first: it is the cheapest way to signal a new era while keeping the name.

Refine a recognized mark that is hard to use (clearer proportions, simpler details, more variations), and replace one that looks dated next to the new owners’ ambition: Airport Executive’s busy circular badge became a compact monogram.

See my logo redesign before-and-after examples and fix your logo guide.

Upgrade typography, color and tone

Type, color and tone carry the new direction into everyday materials.

Change a generic palette, but keep a signature color customers recognize.

Typography is almost always upgraded, because it costs little and lifts everything.

License the fonts for web, print, signage and app, and record them in a style guide.

Reset the tone to match the repositioning: bigger ambitions need calmer, more confident copy and fewer taglines, which is how “Travel with a difference” gave way to “Your chauffeur awaits.”

Rebuild the website even when the domain stays

Keep the domain if the name stays, but rebuild the site, because it is the primary proof of the new era.

Do not let a logo approval stand in for approval of the entire customer experience.

ElementKeep whenChange whenAirport Executive
NameCustomers search for it; reviews carry itFounder’s name, legal issue, platform brandKept
LogoRecognized; works smallDated, busy, weak on vehiclesReplaced: AE monogram
ColorA recognized signature colorGeneric or the old owner’s tasteRed and gray became black, white, gold, gray
TypographyLicensed and on-brandDated or unlicensedNew serif wordmark
Tagline and toneStill true to the offerTied to the old owner’s voiceTagline retired; campaign lines
WebsiteRecently rebuilt, same positioningAnything elseRebuilt

Rebranding case study: Airport Executive under new ownership

Airport Executive is a premium London chauffeur service with more than 25 years in business that needed to rebrand under new ownership to support global expansion plans, so it kept its name and I replaced the logo, typography, palette and website.

What the old identity was holding back

The old logo was a red circular emblem with a roof and stripe motif, a mixed red and gray wordmark and the tagline “Travel with a difference.”

It read as generic travel graphics, and a busy badge does not hold up on vehicles, digital interfaces and small touchpoints.

What changed and what stayed

I replaced the emblem with a monogram.

The new mark is a black AE monogram whose counter-space forms a subtle jet silhouette, paired with a high-contrast serif wordmark.

Around it sit a palette of black, white, gold and gray, a minimalist visual system and a website built to support the company’s global ambition.

The scope was brand strategy, visual identity, motion and web design.

  • Logo system in color variations, business cards, a branded book with acrylic slipcase.
  • Campaign banners: “Arrive in style, depart in comfort.” and “Your chauffeur awaits.”
  • Chauffeur ID badge and lanyard, mobile app icon, website.
  • Vehicle window decal, merchandise, environmental signage, an escalator video.

The name stayed; the way the business presented itself changed.

Chris Nixon of Airport Executive put it this way.

“Arek is a branding expert with extensive experience in graphic design, logos, and web design. We have collaborated with him on several rebranding projects. I highly recommend him.”

See the full Airport Executive case study, the live site, or my branding process, which follows the same project.

What happens to the website, domain and reviews after a sale?

The website, domain, reviews and social accounts transfer with the business, so rename and redirect existing properties and never recreate them: a recreated Google Business Profile starts with no reviews, and a new domain without one-to-one redirects loses its rankings.

Rename and redirect, never recreate

  • Domain: transfer it and the registrar account to the buyer.
  • Redirects: map every old URL to its new one with 301 redirects and keep them, per Google, “as long as possible, generally at least 1 year”; if the domain changes, also submit the Change of Address in Search Console and keep the old domain registered permanently.
  • Google Business Profile: the seller adds the buyer as a manager and transfers primary ownership, then you edit the existing listing.
  • Reviews: Google keeps reviews when the owner changes and the name stays but may treat a big name change as a new business, so announce any rename and keep the old name in the description.
  • Social handles: rename the accounts, re-register the old handle immediately and point it at the new one.
  • Email: add the new domain and forward old addresses for at least a year.
  • Trademarks: confirm they were assigned to the buyer, run a clearance search before adopting a new name or a substantially new logo, then file the new mark.

Rebuild the site alongside the identity

Plan the new site with the identity, so the launch is one event.

A new logo alone will not fix mismatched materials, such as a website, presentation and brochure that each look like a different company, which is where my web design process starts.

How do you roll out a rebrand?

Roll out in four stages: audit in month one, decide and brief in month two, design in months two to four, then switch everything digital on one day and finish the physical rollout, most visible items first, within a year.

My typical ranges: two to four weeks for audit and strategy, four to eight for the identity system, six to twelve for the website, partly in parallel, plus several weeks of signage fabrication.

PhaseTimingOutput
AnnounceDay 1: employees, then customersDay-one message, internal FAQ
Audit and listenDays 1–30: recognition audit, touchpoint inventory, freeze old-brand spendKeep, refine, replace list
Decide and briefDays 30–60: brand path, scope, trademark searchSigned brief and scope sheet
DesignMonths 2–4: identity, website, guidelinesApproved identity, launch checklist
Brand dayMonths 3–6: site, profiles, handles, email, templatesLive site, renamed profiles
Physical rolloutMonths 6–12: vehicles, signage, print; measure inquiries, reviews, retentionCompleted rollout

One launch day for everything digital

I plan brand day like a site launch: redirects tested the night before, then everything digital switched together.

Where old and new materials will coexist, define what acceptable consistency looks like during the transition, and write it into the brand guidelines.

Physical touchpoints in order of visibility

Physical items follow in the order customers see them.

  1. The team: talking points, a one-page FAQ and a short answer for customers who ask what changed.
  2. Vehicle decals and driver ID badges: cheap, visible and fast.
  3. Exterior signage: permits, landlord approval and fabrication take time, so use temporary vinyl.
  4. Uniforms, lanyards, print and packaging: replaced as stock runs out.
  5. Invisible touchpoints: voicemail greetings, contracts, supplier portals and PDF proposals (my branding checklist catches the rest).

Rich Jordan of Highground, a roll-up of nine acquired trades businesses, told customers three times and kept legacy phone numbers live, and I would do the same for the first 90 days.

How much does rebranding after an acquisition cost?

The cost of rebranding after an acquisition depends on scope, not on the deal: a logo refresh with templates costs a fraction of a full identity system, identity plus website is the largest design scope, and physical implementation (signage, fleet decals, uniforms) is a separate budget.

  • Refresh: refined mark, color and type system, templates.
  • Identity: strategy, new logo system, palette, typography, guidelines, core collateral.
  • Identity plus website: all of the above plus site design and build, often with motion and app assets (Airport Executive’s tier).

For current ranges, see my logo design cost guide and branding package guide.

Cost goes up with renaming (trademark filing, new domain, redirects, new signage), several businesses to unify, multiple locations or countries, and rushed timelines.

Cost stays down when you keep the name, domain and a recognized color, launch on one day, and phase physical items with fleet turnover and reprint dates.

Before you ask any designer for a quote, write a scope sheet listing the tier, the touchpoints and the implementation items.

Common mistakes in post-acquisition rebrands

The most common mistakes in a post-acquisition rebrand are about communication and sequencing, not about the logo.

  • Announcing the deal without the brand decision: put the brand promise in the day-one message.
  • Changing name, logo, pricing and systems at once: separate brand continuity from system change, as Capital One kept the Discover brand after the May 2025 acquisition and left customer accounts unchanged at close.
  • Running two brands with no end date: the acquired one tends to decay into a discount tier, as Compaq did under HP, so set a brand day.
  • Framing the change as a sale, not an investment: announce the upgrade, as Airport Executive’s campaign lines sell the experience rather than the change of hands.

My worst rebrands, biggest rebrands and branding mistakes lists have more.

Rebranding after an acquisition: FAQ

These are the questions new owners ask most often.

What is the difference between a brand refresh and a rebrand?

A brand refresh keeps the name and the logo and tidies the system around them, while a rebrand replaces the identity and, in a full rebrand, the name as well.

After an acquisition the usual middle ground is a redesign: same name, new logo, typography, color and website.

What is the difference between rebranding and repositioning a company?

Repositioning changes who the business is for and what it promises, while rebranding changes how the business looks and sounds.

New owners often reposition first, and the rebrand follows only when the old identity no longer fits the new promise (see my brand positioning guide).

Do I have to change the name when I buy a business?

No: when you buy a business, the legal entity and the brand name are separate decisions, and the name is usually the asset you paid for.

Change it for a departing founder’s name, a legal encumbrance or one platform brand (see my company name guide).

Can you keep the same company name but change the logo after an acquisition?

Yes, and for a single small business keeping the company name while replacing the logo is usually the sensible outcome.

The name carries search, review and referral equity; the logo rarely does.

Airport Executive kept its name under new ownership and replaced a red circular emblem with a black AE monogram.

How do you keep brand equity when rebranding after an acquisition?

Keep brand equity after an acquisition by auditing what customers recognize before changing anything, then holding those elements constant.

That means keeping the name, transferring rather than recreating the Google Business Profile and social accounts, and redirecting every old URL for at least a year.

How do you announce a rebrand after an acquisition to customers and employees?

To announce a rebrand after an acquisition, tell employees first, then customers within hours, and say what is not changing: name, team, service, pricing and contacts.

Have the owner call top accounts, pin a notice on the website and profiles, and repeat the message at least three times over the first 90 days.

What should a post-acquisition rebrand brief include?

A post-acquisition rebrand brief should separate the brand decisions already made from the ones still open, and state what to preserve, who approves and what must be ready first.

These are the seven questions I ask.

  1. What is changing in the business, and why now?
  2. Which brand decisions are fixed, and which are open?
  3. What recognition must be preserved?
  4. Must a parent or sister brand appear?
  5. Which pages and physical applications matter most?
  6. Who approves the direction?
  7. What must be ready first, and by when?

Attach the one-page audit, the chosen brand path, touchpoint photos, existing logo files, the trademark status of the name and marks, and fleet and signage deadlines.

Ask the designer to show old and new in comparable applications, such as a vehicle, a card and a site header (see my logo presentation guide).

Expect guidelines and production-ready logo files at handover.

A good rebrand should make the next version of the business clearer without discarding useful recognition by default.

If you have taken over a business and need to decide what to keep, what to change and how to sequence the rollout, that is the work I do.
